Your network card has an unique number that identifies that particular network card, no matter if WiFi or cable. It's called a MAC-address and is usually hard-coded into the card like the registration number stamped into the engine of a car or the serial number on a bike. On a deeper level, this is what decides what information goes where - The IP address is only the top layer.

Let's say that only you and me share a VPN. You want to check out bbc.co.uk, while I want to check out pornhub.com.

Your computer tells the VPN "I'm user bourbonexpert and registering MAC address A. I want to download bbc.co.uk."

My computer does the same, "I'm Uncle420 and registering MAC address B. I want to download pornhub.com".

Now the VPN has two requests, so it connects to the sites - "BBC, send me your webpage in an envelope marked A! Pornhub, send me some sleaze in an envelope marked B!"

VPN gets two packets, each marked for individual recipients. The VPN sends parcel A to you, B to me. You only see the BBC parcel and never know the ropey assholes your copy of the website has traveled alongside with through the VPN.

And as a bonus here is what makes a VPN "secure" against government raids. Lets say user Glenn is connecting to a whistleblowing server to give them some juicy leaks. But oh no, the server was a honey pot!

How do the government track down Glenn? They check the IP address that Glenn connected from. But it leads only to the VPN... So they confiscate the entire physical VPN machine. But here's the magic, the VPN removes the Glenn from the recipients list as soon as he disconnects. So when the G-men tries to see who MAC-address C is registered to... there's literally nothing there.

if a make a purchase of a giant black dildo im still identified, so what difference does it make?

On a privacy-philosophical level, you have chosen to identify yourself. You have not been identified. You can choose not to be identified. That's a whopper of a difference. On a practical user level it's designed to make no difference and is more related to individual privacy which I will explain here:

what exactly is the benefits of a VPN service as opposed to something like "HTTPS everywhere" coupled with a proxy?

It depends on what level of privacy and anonymity you're after. A proxy server works fundamentally different from a VPN, and the most basic HTTP-proxy servers don't handle torrents, only HTTP/S traffic. With a proxy+HTTPS Everywhere your ISP/local neighborhood government can still see what sites you visit (though not details regarding what sub-site i.e. voat.co yes, voat.co/v/technology no), at what time, estimate how long you spend there and so on. A lot is done with a proxy but a lot is left undone as well.

With VPN all anybody can see is that you hooked up the VPN, how much traffic (not type) and for how long.

By the way, HTTPS Everywhere is just a preset list of sites it knows has HTTPS-access. If my new site isn't registered with them, you will still default back to good ol' HTTP. Check out the polar opposite, HTTP Nowhere - It always checks if the site has HTTPS and if not you have the option to block them.

A free proxy/VPN+HTTP Nowhere is the cheapest free solution that has any privacy to it. If you don't pay, you're the product and most "free" privacy services make their money by selling your privacy. That includes Opera and their "VPN", one of the former tech flagship of my country which is now a smudge we don't talk about.

Back to your black dildo. It's basically individual privacy, related to cookies the website sets on your computer. How can you order that fancy new sextoy? You have to register an account.

When you register your account, the website places a cookie (a small snippet of text accessible only to the particular website) on your computer, "This computer belongs to customer bourbonexpert". Every time you visit the website, it knows who you are as long as it finds the cookie. Deleting the cookie stops the site from individually identifying you (at the cost of not being logged in to your customer account).

That's the individual privacy that you maintain with addons such as NoScript, SelfDestructingCookies, LSO killers and so on.

VPN's, proxies and HTTPS defends you against infrastructure privacy breeches.

I normally shit on gaffots like crazy but this one actually has one hell of a point, so I'll just post it here:

The "original design of the game" works in terms of levels, not pits. Levels are collections of obstacles which are connected to one another; it's not "one pit", but dozens of pits, with enemies, tricks, and secrets, all laid out in design choices that are influenced by each other. Two pits in a row =/= two levels made up of just one pit each. Anything that comes before adds meaning (and urgency) to what comes after.

Sounds like I'm saying 1+1, but I'm trying to highlight how just how the original design of the game is greatly changed. For example, a game with one checkpoint per level is hugely influential to how the game is played. If you add a checkpoint before every single challenge, you've completely changed the meaning of each of those challenges and whatever is left of that level. This is to say nothing of just removing an entire limited continue/lives system (either for the whole game or just that level) if it was originally present. If you cut up a level into a independent series of "rooms" or "screens" (in the fashion save-state influenced "masocore" sub-genre, which is the logical(?) end point of this), you have removed the win condition "beat the level" by replacing it with something else.

I realize one may find notions like "real gamer" toxic, but to internalize one's lower skill levels or being afraid of elitism to the point where we can't even discuss basic notions of game design or one's own taste is intellectually toxic. Maybe it's not the people playing hard mode that have fragile egos here.
